chief_complaint: abdominal pain starting at navel moving to RLQ
hpi_details: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with abdominal pain that started as a dull ache around the navel and has migrated to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) over the past 12 hours, now sharp and constant, with associated loss of appetite and mild nausea.
ideas: She thinks she is experiencing severe menstrual cramps or a ruptured ovarian cyst.
concerns: She is worried that she will need emergency surgery and miss her college final exams starting this week.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound to check her ovaries and strong pain relief so she can finish studying.

investigation_events.availability_message: The point-of-care urine pregnancy test is now available.

investigation_events.title: Urgent appendicitis imaging
investigation_events.availability_message: The urgent appendicitis imaging is now available; IV fluids, analgesia, antibiotics, and surgical consultation should not be delayed.

results.value: Noncompressible blind-ending tubular structure measuring 9 mm with periappendiceal echogenic fat and focal probe tenderness; no abscess

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Appendicitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes keeping the patient NPO, IV fluid resuscitation, and urgent surgical consultation for laparoscopic appendectomy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: abdominal pain starting at navel moving to RLQ

Key HPI features: A 20-year-old female presents to the clinic with abdominal pain that started as a dull ache around the navel and has migrated to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) over the past 12 hours, now sharp and constant, with associated loss of appetite and mild nausea.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 37.9C, HR 96, BP 118/74. Abdominal exam reveals tenderness and voluntary guarding at McBurney's point with a positive Rovsing's sign; no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Urine hCG pending. Bloods: WBC 12,500 /uL with left shift.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Appendicitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Gastroenteritis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diffuse rigidity — suggests perforation.
management_principles: Keep the patient NPO, provide IV fluids and analgesia
Obtain urgent general surgery consultation for laparoscopic appendectomy
Counsel the patient on the diagnosis and the need for surgery
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 20-year-old female presents with abdominal pain that started as a dull ache around the navel and has migrated to the right lower quadrant (RLQ) over the past 12 hours, now sharp and constant, with associated loss of appetite and mild nausea.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 37.9C, HR 96, BP 118/74. Abdominal exam reveals tenderness and voluntary guarding at McBurney's point with a positive Rovsing's sign; no rebound or diffuse rigidity. Urine hCG pending. Bloods: WBC 12,500 /uL with left shift.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute appendicitis; gynecologic causes (e.g., ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion) must be excluded given her age and sex.
reference_soap.plan: Keep NPO, establish IV access, provide fluids, analgesia, antiemetics, and urgent surgical assessment. Obtain CBC, urinalysis, and pregnancy testing before imaging/operative planning; use ultrasound and/or CT according to pregnancy status and local pathways. Consider gynecologic causes, including ectopic pregnancy, in the differential before appendectomy.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Acute Appendicitis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Acute Appendicitis
Implement evidence-based management plan: NPO, IV fluids, appendectomy (laparoscopic)

teaching.one_liner: Obstruction of the appendiceal lumen causing pain migrating from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant.
differentials: Ectopic pregnancy / ovarian cyst or torsion

must_ask.say: Did the pain move from your belly button to your lower right side?
Any loss of appetite, nausea, or fever?
Does walking or coughing make it worse?

history.answer: My stomach started aching around my belly button about 12 hours ago, and now the pain has moved down to my lower right side and feels much worse.
It began gradually about 12 hours ago as a dull stomachache, but over the last few hours it became sharp and constant.
At first it was right around my belly button, but then it shifted down to the lower right side of my belly.
No, it stays right there in my lower right abdomen and doesn't shoot to my back, shoulder, or groin.
It started as a dull, crampy ache, but right now it feels like a steady, sharp pain.
Around my belly button it was about a 3 out of 10, but now in the lower right side it is around a 7 out of 10.
Walking around, coughing, or bumping the bed makes it hurt a lot more, so I feel best lying completely still with my legs curled up.
No, I have never had stomach pain like this before.
I completely lost my appetite today and couldn't even think about eating breakfast or lunch.
I felt mildly nauseous after the pain started, but I haven't actually thrown up.
I had a normal bowel movement yesterday morning, and I've passed a little bit of gas today, but no diarrhea or blood.
I've been feeling slightly feverish and warm since this morning, but I haven't had shaking chills.
No, my skin and eyes look normal, and my urine hasn't turned dark.
No burning or pain when I pee, no blood, and I am not going to the bathroom more often than usual.
No, I haven't felt dizzy or faint at all.
No unusual vaginal bleeding, spotting, or strange discharge.
My last period started about two weeks ago, and my cycles are very regular every 28 days.
I am sexually active with my boyfriend, but we always use condoms consistently and my period was totally normal.
No, no chest discomfort, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
I had regular pasta for dinner last night, nothing particularly greasy or spicy, and no alcohol.
I haven't taken any pain medicine, ibuprofen, or aspirin because I didn't want to upset my stomach further.
I don't have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart conditions.
I've never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital before.
I don't take any prescription medications, birth control pills, or supplements.
I don't have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I don't smoke cigarettes, and I've never used e-cigarettes.
I only drink socially, maybe one glass of beer or wine once or twice a month with friends.
I am a college student living in a dormitory with a roommate.
No major health conditions run in my family; my parents and brother are healthy, and no one has bowel diseases.

I thought it was just really bad menstrual cramps or maybe an ovarian cyst acting up. I have college final exams starting in two days, and I'm terrified that needing surgery will make me fail my semester.

exam.finding: The patient appears in moderate discomfort, lying still on the examination bed with her right knee slightly bent.
Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg, pulse 96 beats per minute, temperature 37.9 C, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor; sclerae are white and anicteric.
The abdomen is flat and symmetric with no surgical scars, rashes, distension, or visible peristalsis.
Bowel sounds are present in all four quadrants, though slightly hypoactive, with no abdominal bruits.
Abdomen is soft overall, but there is marked localized tenderness and voluntary guarding at McBurney's point in the right lower quadrant; no diffuse rigidity.
No rebound tenderness is elicited upon gentle release.
Positive Rovsing's sign with referred pain in the right lower quadrant upon palpation of the left lower quadrant, and pain on right psoas stretch.
Negative Murphy's sign with no tender arrest on deep inspiration during right upper quadrant palpation.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.
